Length at metamorphosis in Black drum (Pogonias cromis) is reached when individuals measure approximately 1.2 centimeters , a diminutive size that reflects the species' reliance on a protracted pelagic larval phase before transitioning to demersal habitats. Field collections of ichthyoplankton along the Gulf of Mexico coast indicate that this length corresponds to the completion of fin ray ossification and the onset of juvenile pigmentation patterns. Eclosion occurs from transparent, pelagic eggs that measure roughly 1 millimeter in diameter, and the newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an initial wet weight of just 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams], a value derived from the volumetric relationship of a spherical egg of that diameter. This minimal body mass at birth imposes a narrow window for the lecithotrophic larva to locate suitable prey before the endogenous yolk reserves are fully absorbed. The larval-juvenile transition at 1.2 centimeters  thus marks a critical bottleneck in early survival, as the post-metamorphic juvenile must immediately begin exogenous feeding on small copepods and polychaete larvae in shallow estuarine nursery habitats.

As Black drum approach reproductive competence, the total length at puberty has been estimated at 64.5 centimeters [Lp = 64.5 centimeters], a size typically attained within the first three to four years of life in warm-temperate estuaries of the southeastern United States. Gonadal recrudescence in this species becomes histologically evident when males and females reach approximately this length, coinciding with the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals redirect a substantial portion of their ingested energy toward vitellogenesis and spermiation, a shift that is accompanied by a marked increase in condition factor prior to the first spawning event. The pubertal threshold of 64.5 centimeters [Lp = 64.5 centimeters] places Black drum among the larger scienids to delay maturity, a life-history strategy that is likely tied to their extended lifespan and the need to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support repeated, high-fecundity spawning events over multiple seasons. Field otolith analyses confirm that most fish in exploited populations become vulnerable to the fishery before reaching this size, raising concerns about the demographic sustainability of harvests skewed toward immature individuals.

The reproductive output of Black drum is substantial, with females producing an average of approximately 19,178 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 19,178 eggs per day] when maintained under stable thermal conditions of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], a temperature that approximates typical spring spawning temperatures in the northern Gulf of Mexico. This daily rate was calculated from a kap value of 0.90, reflecting a high proportion of ingested energy channeled toward gamete production in mature adults, but the empirical basis lies in batch fecundity estimates from gravid females captured during peak spawning aggregations. At 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], the species exhibits a protracted spawning season extending from February through May, during which individual females may release multiple batches of pelagic eggs at intervals of several days. The high daily fecundity of approximately 19,178 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 19,178 eggs per day] compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the early planktonic stages, where egg predation and advection from suitable nursery habitats can eliminate over 99 percent of the offspring before settlement. This bet-hedging strategy is typical of large-bodied, iteroparous scianids that inhabit dynamic estuarine environments.

Ultimate total length in Black drum has been documented to reach 170 centimeters [Li = 170 centimeters], a formidable size that places this species among the largest members of the family Sciaenidae. Individuals approaching this asymptotic length are typically several decades old and exhibit a characteristically robust body morphology, with a deep, compressed trunk and a blunt snout adapted for bottom-feeding on mollusks and crustaceans. The corresponding adult body mass at this maximum size is approximately 51,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 51,800 grams], though the heaviest individuals are almost exclusively females, reflecting pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this species. These massive adults play an important ecological role as top benthic predators in Gulf of Mexico seagrass beds and oyster reefs, where their foraging activity can structure invertebrate community composition. The attainment of 170 centimeters in length is rare in contemporary populations due to decades of intensive commercial and recreational fishing pressure, which has truncated the size distribution and reduced the mean age of spawning adults. Size-selective harvest has likely imposed strong selective pressure for earlier maturation, though the genetic basis of this shift remains poorly resolved.

Maximum lifespan in Black drum, derived from otolith annulus counts of the oldest individuals collected in relatively unfished populations, reaches approximately 43 years [am = approximately 43 years] under the thermal regime of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C] typical of their subtropical range. This longevity is among the highest reported for any scianid from the western Atlantic and is comparable to that of the closely related red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus), though Black drum achieve a considerably larger ultimate body size. The extended lifespan of 43 years [am = 43 years] is associated with a slow pace of senescence, likely mediated by the relatively low metabolic demands of a benthic, molluscivorous diet and the absence of high-energy pursuit predation at a temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. At 23.5 °C, growth in length decelerates markedly after the first decade, with annual increments shrinking to less than 2 centimeters per year beyond age twenty. The combination of late maturity, high fecundity, and extreme longevity is characteristic of a k-selected life-history strategy that evolved in the relatively stable, food-rich environments of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal shelves, though it renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation when harvest pressure is elevated.
